blocks.x: I'd like to ask you first of all is how you started playing around what time that was and with what band you first started playing about 23

started out following Chris Kelly's band, Wooden Jewels, Lions Band, Cuckoo, Buddy Petit, points of, I was a kid, but actually I mean played with during that time like followed Chris Kelly, set and played with him, Wooden Jewels,
and René and the kids was going set and played. In 23, how old were you then?

I was around about 18 years old. I was living around Marigny and Ramport there. We used to be a little depot there. They used to run down Point Lash Exclusion down there. Chris Kelly and all. They used to play down there. They used to have baptism down there in Exclusion. The train used to run down there. Used to hop off it, pick blackberries, and get back on it and ride down there. About 40 miles would take you a night and a day to get out there. So you just got to get back on it.
Was there anybody in particular who taught you to play your instrument, trumpet? Not right off the reel.

I just flew around with the horn and used to put a kuzit, one of the kuzit, and just blowed like I was playing the trumpet. Mark beats the trumpet and every year, the kuzit, the kuzit. And Faisal and I got around Chris and them. He told me to come to his house and taught me how to try to blow it. Didn't have much time to waste with me. Every time I blew that wood we go, I'd start to drink. That was the most of the thing, was drinking. In fact, I got a little more experience from Wooden Joe because I used to go by his house. We'd stay there and I'd have more time with him. Oh, yes. And try and learn how to execute the horn I did with Chris because Chris was mostly to get there and we'd just go out and have a little fun playing and that was it. That was the lesson. That was the lesson.
But before we go on, I'm sure if I would ask for Mr. Kuller somewhere among the musicians, nobody would know your name. Your name actually among musicians is Sheik, isn't it?
Sheik, that's right.
And how did you get that name?

Well, I'd say I was around about 17 years old and the Cloud Gable suit was out with the arrows all around him and I used to wear them suits, pants and pockets, arrows all around them and the children and most people said, look at the Sheik, look at the Sheik. Well, it was Sheik. It just went on, went on and up until now. Nobody knows me, my Sheik. If it wasn't, people would know me way back if you'd come to the place and ask for George Kuller.
Yeah, that's actually the name of those suits.

Yeah, it was at that time. The Sheik suits. It was arrows all around and arrows all around the time. And even today, it's places where I'd be right now and you'd come in and see, you'd see on George Kuller, nobody would know. It wouldn't be real old time, you know. But if you say Sheik, everybody would say right now. Yeah, he was here, he left, he went.

And in those early days in the 20s when you first started playing, who would you say were the musicians that made the strongest impression on you? Well, I tell you, it was Chris Kelly. Chris Kelly. Yeah.

See, at that time, most of it was blues. And Chris Kelly was the man that looked like my ambition made me more on the trumpet, cause I always wanted to play the blues like him. And anywhere he would play, I mean the people, they said to say Chris was there and that was a lot of people, they said to say, you know, he was a regular fella and I mean he was public like him more because he drank and all of them, this was a regular guy. And he played what they wanted. And the way he played there, that's what they wanted. He said Chris, he didn't have no trouble. Okay, what other band was around there when they said Chris, that was it.
What made him technically so famous? Did he use any particular mutes or something? Or did he always play a straight horn?

Well, no, he had a, mostly, just like I said, it was a mute, it's called a flusher then. Wah wah, he used that on like careless love and all that and he just could make it cry. You see, just make it cry. And he had a, in fact, another little mute would go all the way in the horn. See, he used the cornets then, the bell was big, you see. And the little mute that he used in would go all the way in there and for the other mute, the flusher, could fit over that and he'd get the effect from the mute and from the flusher. And the way he could execute the mute would bring the flusher, the way he could execute the flusher would bring the mute out with it and make it sound anyway like a baby crying or she was hollering and serious. I mean, this man would make it cry. He must have been very powerful then to be able to use two mutes. He didn't use it in a, I mean, in a, say like a broad tone, he'd use it in a keen tone with it and it seemed like he'd have the flusher so tight in there that he could just do what he want in a tight move. You know, like a broad, you'd give a blast and he didn't have anything, that's what he'd cry. And all these chores would be out there and wouldn't be mad. And sometimes he'd just use his dub and things, you know what I mean? I used to have the men and the way he'd play it in the stop time movement and all, and he's crying. And then, women just throw their pocketbook at it. Just dance, man. Just get so, you know, excited. Throw their pocketbook at it. But they had, I mean, other fellows, I mean, it was great during that time. Rene and Buddy Petit and all those fellows. But when Chris, they say Chris was around that, was that? Mm-hmm. That was it. Yeah.
Did you hear Louis Dumaine play a lot also?

Louis Dumaine swung as this, swung as this. He used to play at the Royal Garden. Remember I was a kid and the Royal Garden was on Drive, between Drive and Rampart. And he had a nice band. Nice band, I mean. Wasn't no Bauhaus, you know. No, he wasn't no Bauhaus. He played nice music, wasn't no Bauhaus. You see the fellows I'm talking about now was Bauhaus, really strictly Bauhaus.
What were some of the places where they played that? Oh. Where Chris Kelly would be found. Imagine if there were tourists I got in 1927 in New Orleans, I'd like to hear Chris Kelly.

Well, he used to be down there. We used to have a place called the Sawdison, way down where the cattle would be at. A little room right down there next to the cattle pen, down Seminole. Go in there and play. And they'd play Flood Street. We used to have a dance in the mud out there. I was living on a marinerie between St. Claude and Rampart. A fellow that called Willie White. Used to have parties in his yard right next door to my house. And Chris Kelly used to play there. Chris Kelly used to come there before they start. I used to have my horn next door. Blurring my horn like that. Just warm it up there. Just warm it up there. He'd hear me. All right, son. Son. Okay. You'll be all right. You'll be all right. And he'd get on and thing. He'd play there and I'd go over there. Come on, sit down, sit down. He'd go and leave me there. He'd play the blues. I used to have a number. Clap here and Yuckum Charlie. That was how I'd been. And Kellis Lovewell. I was getting that down. That was my famous. I always loved it the way he, you know. He'd play it. And I just said, it was a number I loved. I used to try to imitate him playing. And finally, I got it down, you know, like I wanted, you know what I mean. I used to use a glass mule derby. Then I even got one of them clutches on him. And we, uh, I did a nice job. I went on his work. And I played Rockford Lewis. That was way, I was around, I was around about, I was around about 18 years old then. I got a job, Rockford Lewis. And he just had a, built a new hall there. And, uh, so, well, I couldn't play that many numbers, I think. And, uh, so I got Chris Kelly with my band. Me, Chris Kelly, Eddie Summers, Leo Montrell, Phillip Gilbert, and the girls sing on that, uh, Irene Watson, Joe Watson, niece kind of player. His niece, she, she had sing, Chris in the hall there. Reverend Moehead was the pastor of that church. He was an old father. He died at about a hundred when he died. And then, uh, about 10, 12 years, around about a hundred when he died. And we christened that hall. It was my job. And I got Chris to play with me, you know, on that job. And we advertised all around on the truck that day. Rockford Lewis, uh, had the hall in charge. And we just went all around and advertised. All the uptown, downtown, all around. And we and Chris played together and all. It was really, it was, it was nice. Nice anywhere Chris was, it was nice. Chris could take any band to this school and so long he'd be there. That's all. That's all. That's all. Yeah, that was great. Worked at Wooden Joe, nice, nice from the player. Nice and all that. In fact, I got more experience, I mean, at the horn, at Wooden Joe and I got more, uh, at all the fellas. Actually, I mean, for learn how to blow the horn and things, you know, because he took more pain with me. And I'd go to his house and we'd spend the whole evening there strictly on blowing the horn, you see. Well, see, when Joe was a fella, he wouldn't do much drinking at the house. And, uh, most he'd drink if he'd be out playing on the job, you see. Well, he'd get off on the job and drink. But, I mean, it just was a business with him. He'd come to his house and, uh, you know, he didn't worry about that. And a pen and mirror, I'll never forget, years ago, he said, you know, my man, knew me, knew all my family and all. Family for, I was born and knew him. But I didn't, go ahead, sorry. I just come to knew him since I was, this, had took up music then. But when I met him, he had knew all my people.

And in those days, um, who were some of your other favorite musicians? For example, who was your favorite clarinet player then? Or the one that made the strongest impression on you whom you ever heard?

Well, I tell you, uh, at that time, George, your boy, was a clarinet player, really admired clarinet. In fact, uh, he was, uh, uh, I mean, uh, more, had been playing along with George, with George, uh, I believe, came up behind him. And George was waiting, Rene and all, and all, and all, and Punch was, I mean, uh, George was working with Punch and then when they was growing, and Punch was mostly famous before George was. And he was playing, playing, playing, playing at me. You know, you see, George mostly, always, he could play, but he never, you know, had the chance with the different bands. Well, he worked with Rene, and that gave him about most of that time the most best, you know, chance that he had. And, you know, Rene a while, and he left and all, you know what I mean? But way back, that was, uh, before George had even was, you know, playing, you know, playing clarinet. George the Boyd was playing, we got Milton Boyd, all that was old, and George the Boyd, they sat on the rail, and this played, different kind of played, they said bands, right, six and seven bands out there. Yeah. Every Sunday out there. All them bands was out there. And they were playing, and they were playing, and they were playing, and they were playing, and they were playing. None of them, I mean, some swell musicians, no, but they didn't, couldn't play no clarinet, and George the Boyd. Yeah, the style, the way he's playing, you know, fit in the band, and this, you know. Most any fella would tell you, you know.
Is there any clarinet player, nowadays, or a clarinet player, who was fortunate enough to get on records, whose style reminds you of George the Boyd's clarinet?

Well, I'd say right now, see, George the Boyd was a clarinet player playing a thing, you know. Nice toarnation, you know. And right now, I mean, just like I'd figure, well, George Lewis is, I mean, is playing, uh, Planet Client at Moe Client at, and what George the Boyd's playing during the time, because George was playing better, but the time, advanced it, and the company got faster, and George is playing Planet Client. Oh, yes, yes, yes. And I will say, at the time when George the Boyd was playing, he was playing Planet Client at George the Boyd. But right now, I'd say George Lewis is, is the Planet Client player.

No, but I mean, somebody whose style reminds you of George the Boyd. For example, if you hear records of Jimmy Noon, or of Johnny Dodds, or some, somebody else, is there somebody who would remind you somehow, the style of George the Boyd?

No, see, George the Boyd, he's still got the New Orleans style, and George Lewis, they just say, that variation, they just, you know, they say, I mean, I could almost tell, uh, uh, uh, uh, take a Planet player, if he's not from New Orleans, I can mostly tell his style of playing, because I know the average, uh, the Planet player style would've been playing. I know George the Boyd style, Boyd Banks style, Reddick on me, all them fellas style. And, uh, George the Boyd and George Lewis mostly varies, fast varies, you know what I mean? I would play it on, you know, almost on the same style. Same style.
So we've had a few trumpet players you mentioned, a few clarinet players, and what about trombone players, who stuck in your mind as being truly remarkable?

Well, I mean, during the time back, uh, what I remember, and the trombone players I was around, and, uh, I'll tell you, out all of them, I mean, uh, uh, uh, uh, uh, a fella was amazed to me on trombone was Harrison Bradley. Harrison Bradley. And he worked at Brinn-Renné for years and all, but he was, I mean, really, a good trombone player. He had everything it take to be a trombone player. I mean, he had every technique, tone, anything. I mean, he never did get excited on it and all. He was just right there. Everything it take to be a trombone player. I wish they had fellas during that time playing the trombone, but, I mean, they wasn't playing the trombone that he was playing. I mean, he was playing the trombone player. Buddy Petit, Kid Renné, all the most good. Nice, pal.

Yeah, he played it as an inch. Talking about Kid Renné, what was in, in those days when his lip was real hard and all that, when he was really in his heyday, what was his strongest point, what was his specialty? Was it out in the streets, or was it playing the blues, or was it playing jitney dance as fast as...

Oh no, see, Renné never did work with no jitney dancer. No, he never did work with that. All of his work was economy hall, copper, and his dance meetings. He never did work with them jitney, he never did work with that. He was a dance hall, advertising, Perez, and all. He never worked at that. And he was a standout man in all his execution. Any number, he was a standout man. He had to like to hear him play . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . clean trumpet players out on them fellas. I wouldn't say he was the best trumpet player, but I mean he was mostly clean, you know, trumpet players because just like I said, they had fellas who would meet him on the street and would run him, you know, like Chris Geller would meet him like that. And I mean he just had to pull off and go, and the people would, but Chris was playing with the people. Rene would play at them different halls and he had this crowd, I mean, I don't know why he's playing. But if Chris playing somewhere and he's playing there, well is this Chris gonna have to, you know what I mean, buddy, the teeth and the punch and all that stuff. I mean that's one of the things, but Rene was one of the sweetest trumpet players, I mean, he was playing dances and things that you know, but the fellas was playing a different type of music from him, I see. He wasn't no, say no ragtime, you know what I mean, no low-round blues player. He played the blues, but he had class with it, you know what I mean, that's the style of playing, you know. He'd be playing, you know, the same blues, but I mean he was, he wasn't a sailor, I don't know. I mean, sweet, sweet. Vegetable Packers, he used to, every Sunday, Square Deals and all that's a club that he used to play for the high deals and all that. See, three poor bands out on the truck, come out. Sometimes Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, Kid Rene, all of them meet up on the corner together, advertising for three different dances, three different dances. And all the people behind them and they call everybody with their prayer and they just stay there and play. Chris gonna be there when the deal goes down. Chris gonna be, Chris gonna shoot that cannon. I mean, that's it. That's it. I mean, that's what I didn't do was to play. I mean, but when they dance at night, they have this and have their bunch and I don't have their bunch. They just work the way it was different. People say, well, I'll put it this way, just like they did with the brass band. You have some people say, well, I'm gonna go behind the Ricker band. And some say, I'm going behind the Tuxedo. Some say, I'm going behind the Gibson. Well, at that time, people say, well, I'm Chris. Well, Chris had the most of favorites cause he had the blues bunch. Now you take Rene had plenty of bunch because the club would never give that with his plan for. They had different types of people and they favored Rene. And it was what everybody had their own, you know.
Was Buddy Petit still very active in those things?
Well, yeah, he was at his best. He was at his best, yeah. He was at his best.
What was his typical style of playing or his favorite type of music?

Oh, he was, well, Buddy, he was a fellow who would play. He didn't worry about, you know, high notes and all, but he played so sweet. Everything he played was in the staff and it was sweet. I mean, everything was sweet. I played with Buddy on his last, when he was down, on his last go around. And I played with him several jobs, you know, and he played second trumpet. He's a sweet second trumpet player. And I played a couple of jobs with him, you know. And he was living right there on St. Philip and St. Lord, right across from Caldo and upstate. Around what time was that? Oh, I've been so long, so many, I can't remember. But, I mean, Lewis came down here. Lewis was here at the field, you know. And I was at the field, played the field for him.
It was shortly before his death. It was shortly before Buddy Petit's death that you were playing those jobs with him.

Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah, shortly. Well, I mean, he had got sick, you see. When he was at his best, well, I wasn't, you know, I just was coming along, you know. And I remember. But, I mean, shortly before that and all, well, I had yard party jobs, you know. He would take him and he'd play, you know, second trumpet. He was getting sick and weak, you know. But he could play, you know. He would play down there and played several jobs. He was living right upstairs over the Tri-Me Hall there, St. Gordinson, Philly, right across from Caldwell. That's where he died.
Before we go on, I would like to ask Mr. Russell whether he has any questions to ask sheep.
I was wondering, have you ever heard Keppert and Oliver down here in person when you were by?

Never did. Never did. Yeah. But, uh, the most honored of Keppert and Oliver's were, what I've been hearing these days. Oh, man. Uh, during that time, I might have seen them and things, but I can't remember anything.
Can you remember much about Frankie Dooson in his old days?
Never.
You don't remember. He played a long time.

Yeah. I mean, this is where the name of them fellas now. And, I mean, maybe at that time, I might have seen them because I remember Emmanuel Perez, we had the band, and I was going to school. I was about four years old, and I mean, I'm fifty now, so I mean, but I can't play since I can't play. Not like Yank. I know Yank as good as I, I mean, I know you. And he was way back in that time playing tramo. You remember Yank?

Could you tell us a little bit about the brass bands when you heard them when you were a boy? Did they sound about like the Eureka and the bands today, or were they a little different type, bigger or smaller? They were bigger.

You see, the bands then you take a manual prayer, cellist there, all the bands. They had baritone horns, and they had them alto horns, and mostly brass, and what is now, they Hollywood C saxophone, C malaphone and all that nice. And I would see saxophone clarinets. I mean, they was always big. They said, like, we used ten now, they had about fifteen, because it really actually was brass. Everything was brass. You see, outside the clarinets, they didn't have no sax. I mean, all the thing was brass, but the reading, they mostly had was E flat clarinets. Joe Otkin, all those, that's what they played, the clarinets. Did it take reading musicians? Yeah, first class musicians. All of them bands. Tuxedo, Ormwood band, Imperial band, a salsa band. First class band. Pacific band. All of them, first class band.
Did they mostly read music, or did some of them do like they do now? Strictly musicians.
All of them. Strictly music. I mean, this, I mean, like marches, and I mean, like, we do now, like, we go in there with a hymn, you know, and coming back.
Well, did they play many hymns when you were a boy? Somebody told me they didn't play them until about the time that Sam Morgan began playing his hymns with his dance band.

You know, all I knew, like, this same routine like we do now, they leave the hall or something, hymns all the way to the house, they get to the body in the cemetery. They go bind, bind, bind. Yeah, all that. And when they get to, when they get to the body, that's when the field marches come. And they get to the cemetery after that, and they just hymns right along. And same routine with never, no change. They never, they play no marches or nothing until they get the body. They always, this hymns walking fast and all. And come, you see, when they meet the body, with slow film marches. But until they meet the body, this was going along, hymns and things. And when they torn the body loose, they did the same thing like they do now, just play anything. And so, then you're an ambulance, I said, it's on your own. And it's been the same routine since we knew.
If you have a minute yet, could you tell a little bit about when you joined the Eureka Band? Was that the first brass band you played, or any other band?

No, I worked with Willie Parker way back in the present time. Oh, well before I went, no, oh man, way before World War II. El Nero Club, we got $10 in, we spent $10. Incredible, that. The count of a day, now they paid $35 and $40. And this went up there, Willie Parker, and we played, and me, Willie Parker. Howard was with us, and this mix of bands. Willie Manhattan was, the thing was, you know, slow then. I mean, I believe Larry was with us too, and he had got with the Eureka Band too, but he quit the Eureka Band. And, well, him and Willie was good friends, and we just went up there and played.
When did you join the Eureka?

When did you join the Eureka? When did you see, I came out, I must have joined the Eureka around in about, a lot of part of 46, I mean. Because Richardson was playing with them, and every time Richardson was to be there, he wasn't there, and they'd call me and things, so eventually they just took me in the band there. But I waited, or way back, but Renier used to have a brass band, you know, just pick up, you know, started a band, and I worked with him, you know what I mean. I wasn't, you know, this was coming along, you know, at that time. See, at that time, a fella was that good that he could help you, you know what I mean. He was going along, because all the bands was working then, you see, and the fella didn't have a regular band, well, he'd have to pick up some money. Well, he can, I'm working with, you know, that fella.
Didn't you, at one time, play with George Lewis?
Well, yeah, I worked with George, I worked with George before, before Herbert Moran, and before Cuckoo.
Oh, yeah.

You see, I worked with George back at Benefit and St. Rock, and I had my band on the side, you see. At that time, I couldn't make it with George, because I had my little side band, you see. And we worked right there a good while, but after that, I had jobs, that well, uh, um, Loran, he's got my band, well, he stood there a good while, you know, the way he, you know, he likes to drink, playing and all, so, uh, I guess George had to, you know, make a chance, so that's when, uh, Cuckoo got in the band.
Cuckoo, that's, uh, Matawba.

Yeah, yeah, and he got in there when he was with George, and he stood with George, you know, until he passed, and he worked at us a couple of times in our brass band, he worked at me, he worked at me. While he's working, you know, when he's working out there, and every night there, like, uh, like, the Pat Alfredo's working. At Morocco?
Yeah.

Yeah, and he'd wake in, uh, you remember when Cuckoo worked at Cutler, George? I was with the brass band, and he'd wake us, and that was, last time I worked with George was, uh, at Benefit and Central. The day before morning, I worked with him more, about six months, just off now, and he was just working there, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and we worked there.
Any more questions? Uh, you might tell us a little bit about the organization of the Eureka, I mean, the three trumpets, what are the jobs of the three trumpets? Do they have?

They have three trumpets, and all of them have a job. All of us have a job, they do. And the way we operate, uh, we start off three trumpets, and we play the chorus down, and, uh, well, we'll leave, say, two trumpets, the second chorus, you see. Then the two trumpets take down, and then one trumpet will take up. We try to keep one trumpet up at all times, and, uh, when we get ready to go out, then we bring in the whole three trumpets, you see. That's, in order that would have a melody, a lead going at all times for the rest of the bands. So we couldn't afford for the, the whole two trumpets to keep up the whole while, come we'll have to play a number, 15 or 20 minutes, we have now, so we could just do that, and then everybody have a chance to get a break, you know.
And was that, was that the same in the old, in the old days, also the old larger brass.

Oh yeah, they all work on that, you see. Always work on that system. See, they never burn one another out, you know. If you're playing a film, well, they don't hold the film much as long as they hold a head number, you see because it's help when you're playing from the music everybody's part is there you got to go along with it you see but if you're playing this coming back or going on there a head number well I mean everybody in the band understand and you could always keep somebody candle on to help the other fellas out of leads something to go by you see I have something to go by this a little lead and they they can just do what they want but there's somebody carrying the melody and everybody waits for me
how often do you have regular rehearsals?

no rehearsals no rehearsals on this time a rehearsal you see if we got something special coming up and the people want certain numbers you know what I mean and we call a rehearsal well to get that together a special something they want but outside that you know rehearsal

but today for example that Clark was telling me he had ordered a march a march of Bond Mandeli march something if that march arrived and I thought he likes it somebody else like then he will have a rehearsal

if he calling he might don't call he'll have this bringing he do that every time I mean we have funeral marches we have never played just come on the street and he say I got this and we just go on and play which they have men's capable to play I mean have men to play any music that they bring have real men's capable but for Herschel it's good but I mean it never happens that we have to do that just like I say the only thing they might call a rehearsal person well if there's something big going on the people just want a certain special number and all they might just you know call us and but I but this is a bar in music and they get marches we don't have to say just come bring it and that's it didn't seem like they get a kick out of it that's it and they do a nice job out of it
when you first started I guess you started just using your head by ear you didn't

yeah this is by air this nobody in my family haven't played any music and I used to go to dance parties in the yard and listen to different bands and they had old beat up cornette some fella gave me that cornette and I used to put a little crusade in it just like I said see you just don't wait the keys on this boy you know because they put little soup paper then I went on long time with that until I got around this and on the fellas and they seen I was interested in this one come to hard way you played any other instrument before trumpet you ever wanted to no not say uh played it but I mean I'd fool around with this one like drums I mean I know the time and I just want to play piano to play blues
